title: Deriving a reduction formula
problem: Let $I_n = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx$. Derive the reduction formula $I_n = \dfrac{n-1}{n}\,I_{n-2}$.

steps.instruction: Write $\sin^n x$ as a product and apply integration by parts.
steps.working: Write $\sin^n x = \sin^{n-1}x \cdot \sin x$. Let $u = \sin^{n-1}x$ and $dv = \sin x\,dx$, so $du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx$ and $v = -\cos x$. $I_n = \Big[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi/2} + (n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x\,dx$

steps.instruction: Evaluate the boundary term and substitute $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$.
steps.working: The boundary term vanishes at both limits. $I_n = (n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x(1 - \sin^2 x)\,dx = (n-1)(I_{n-2} - I_n)$

steps.instruction: Apply the formula again to find $I_5$.
Check the result is consistent with $\{I_n\}$ being a decreasing sequence.
steps.working: $\frac{8}{15} \approx 0.533$. This is less than $I_4 \approx 0.589$ and greater than $I_6 \approx 0.491$, which is consistent since $\{I_n\}$ is decreasing. ✓

steps.instruction: Recognise the form of the integrand and choose a substitution.
steps.working: The integrand has the form $[\text{function of }\ln x]\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}$, which suggests the substitution $u = \ln x$, so $du = \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$.
